stem: Jonas takes his laptop to a conference. Which kind of Linux machine is that?

options.text: A server, because it is a computer with a keyboard and a screen
options.rationale: Servers are set up to provide services, often with no screen.

options.text: An embedded system, because it is portable
options.rationale: Embedded systems are built into a product with one fixed job.

options.text: An HPC cluster, because it has more than one core
options.rationale: Clusters link many servers into one machine.

options.text: A laptop, one of the desktop and mobile computers that run Linux
options.rationale: Laptops run the same desktop distributions as PCs, such as Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora.

explanation: Desktops, laptops and mobile devices (phones and tablets, mostly Android) are the machines people use directly.

stem: Which machine is typically managed remotely and has no screen or keyboard?

options.text: A server
options.rationale: Servers run services such as web or build servers and are managed over the network.

options.text: A desktop
options.rationale: Desktops have a screen and keyboard because people use them directly.

options.text: A tablet
options.rationale: Tablets are used directly through a touch screen.

options.text: A smart phone
options.rationale: Phones are used directly through a touch screen.

explanation: Server computers provide services to other machines, and usually work without a screen or keyboard.

stem: Which statement about an HPC cluster is correct?

options.text: It is a single small device built into a product, with one fixed job.
options.rationale: That describes an embedded system.

options.text: It is a virtual machine rented by the hour.
options.rationale: That describes a cloud instance.

options.text: It joins many servers, called nodes, to work together on one big job.
options.rationale: Weather, science and AI workloads run on clusters, and nearly all the biggest supercomputers run Linux.

options.text: It is a laptop with a very fast graphics card.
options.rationale: A laptop is a single machine for one user.

explanation: HPC stands for high-performance computing. The cluster’s nodes share one job.

stem: Which of these devices is an embedded system?

options.text: A rented cloud instance.
options.rationale: It is a virtual server.

options.text: A router built to do one job.
options.rationale: Embedded systems are small and have one fixed job, and Linux is popular in them.

options.text: A laptop with a docking station.
options.rationale: It is a general-purpose computer.

options.text: A node of a supercomputer.
options.rationale: Nodes belong to an HPC cluster.

explanation: Routers, TVs, cars, cameras and smart home devices contain computers with one fixed job; Linux is common in them.

stem: Ada opens a web page in her browser. Which statement describes the roles?

options.text: The browser is the server, because it shows the page to the user on the screen.
options.rationale: A server waits for requests and provides the service.

options.text: Both programs are servers, since they run on computers.
options.rationale: The browser asks for the page, which makes it the client.

options.text: The web server is the client, because it receives the request.
options.rationale: A client is the one that makes the request.

options.text: The browser is the client that asks, and the web server answers.
options.rationale: A client asks, and a server answers.

explanation: The same computer can be a client for one service and a server for another.

stem: Mira wants to test a risky update on a copy of a whole server, with its own operating system and kernel, without touching real hardware. What fits best?

options.text: A container that shares the host’s kernel
options.rationale: A container shares the kernel, so it doesn’t contain a full operating system.

options.text: A virtual machine running on a hypervisor
options.rationale: A hypervisor gives each VM its own pretend hardware and complete operating system.

options.text: A second user account on the same system
options.rationale: An account shares the same system and kernel.

options.text: A shell script that backs up the home directory
options.rationale: A script copies files and does not provide a second system.

explanation: A VM contains a whole operating system with its own kernel; a container contains an application.

stem: What is the main difference between a container and a virtual machine?

options.text: A container shares the host’s kernel; a VM runs its own operating system.
options.rationale: This is why containers start quickly and take little space.

options.text: A container needs its own hypervisor, but a VM does not.
options.rationale: VMs need a hypervisor; containers don’t.

options.text: A container runs a whole operating system of its own, but a VM runs only one app.
options.rationale: It is the other way round.

options.text: A container only runs on phones, and a VM only on servers.
options.rationale: Both run on servers and desktops.

explanation: Docker and Podman are well-known container tools. A VM contains a whole operating system, a container only an application and its files.

stem: Which cloud service level gives you virtual servers, disks and networks that you set up yourself?

options.text: SaaS, software as a service
options.rationale: SaaS is a finished application, such as webmail.

options.text: PaaS, platform as a service
options.rationale: PaaS is a ready environment to run your code.

options.text: IaaS, infrastructure as a service
options.rationale: IaaS rents the building blocks, such as a cloud instance running Debian.

options.text: HPC, high-performance computing
options.rationale: HPC is a type of cluster, not a cloud service level.

explanation: IaaS rents infrastructure, PaaS a platform for your code, and SaaS a finished application.

stem: Which statement describes cloud computing?

options.text: You buy your own servers and run them in the basement of the office.
options.rationale: That is running your own hardware.

options.text: You install every program from a USB stick, one machine after another.
options.rationale: Installing from USB has nothing to do with the cloud.

options.text: You rent computing power over the internet and pay for what you use.
options.rationale: Capacity can be added or removed quickly.

options.text: You use only programs that run in a single browser tab on one computer.
options.rationale: Browser apps may be hosted in the cloud, but that is not what defines it.

explanation: Cloud computing means renting servers, storage and databases instead of owning them.

stem: Why do many companies choose Linux for their servers?

options.text: It only works with hardware from one single vendor, which has to be paid for in advance.
options.rationale: Linux runs on many kinds of hardware.

options.text: It is free to run, stable and secure, and can be fixed by anyone with the skills.
options.rationale: These properties suit web and cloud use.

options.text: It needs a new licence fee for every user and for every machine of the company.
options.rationale: Linux is free to run.

options.text: It can only run one program at a time, so many machines are needed.
options.rationale: Linux runs many programs at once.

explanation: Linux is used for web servers, clouds, phones, embedded devices and supercomputers. Virtualization lets one machine run many VMs, which saves money.

stem: Webmail, an online office suite and other finished applications that run in the provider’s data center belong to which cloud service level?

options.text: IaaS, infrastructure as a service for virtual servers
options.rationale: IaaS rents virtual servers, disks and networks.

options.text: PaaS, platform as a service for your own code
options.rationale: PaaS rents a ready environment to run your code.

options.text: HPC, high-performance computing clusters
options.rationale: HPC is a cluster type, not a cloud service level.

options.text: SaaS, software as a service
options.rationale: SaaS delivers a finished application over the internet.

explanation: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are the three common cloud service levels.

stem: Which text editor runs in the terminal, lists its key commands at the bottom of the screen and lets you type text right away?

options.text: nano
options.rationale: nano is the easy editor; `^X` means Ctrl+X to exit.

options.text: vi
options.rationale: vi has modes, so you must press `i` before typing text.

options.text: LibreOffice Writer
options.rationale: Writer is a graphical word processor.

options.text: Thunderbird
options.rationale: Thunderbird is an email client.

explanation: nano is the beginner-friendly editor; vi is the powerful, modal one that exists almost everywhere.

stem: Mira opens a file in `vi` and starts typing, but nothing appears the way she expects. Why?

options.text: vi can only edit files that are already open in nano at the very same time.
options.rationale: The editors are independent.

options.text: vi needs the file to be saved under a name before anything can be typed.
options.rationale: Mode, not saving, is the issue.

options.text: vi only edits graphical files such as images and drawings.
options.rationale: vi edits text files in the terminal.

options.text: vi starts in normal mode, where keys are commands; `i` starts insert mode.
options.rationale: vi is a modal editor.

explanation: In vi, Esc returns to normal mode, `i` starts insert mode, `:wq` saves and quits and `:q!` quits without saving.

stem: In `vi`, which command typed in normal mode saves the file and quits the editor? Type the colon command.
explanation: `:wq` writes the file and quits. `:q!` quits without saving.

stem: Ada checks that both editors are installed in the guest. What does this command print?
explanation: `type` shows how the shell would run each name. Both `vi` and `nano` are programs under `/usr/bin` in the guest.

stem: Which statements about vi and nano are true? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: vi has modes, such as normal mode and insert mode.
options.rationale: vi is a modal editor.

options.text: nano shows its key commands on screen, and `^X` exits it.
options.rationale: nano is the easy editor.

options.text: vi is a graphical editor that only works on a desktop.
options.rationale: vi runs in the terminal.

options.text: nano is installed only on Enterprise Linux.
options.rationale: nano is found on many distributions.

options.text: Both editors close without asking when you press Ctrl+C.
options.rationale: That isn’t how they exit.

explanation: You only need awareness: which editors exist, that nano is easy, and that vi is modal and nearly always available.

stem: Mira must install the same software and set the same files on twenty new build machines. Which kind of tool is built for this?

options.text: A configuration management tool, such as Ansible
options.rationale: You describe the wanted state in files and apply it to many machines.

options.text: A text editor, such as nano
options.rationale: nano edits one file at a time.

options.text: A web browser, such as Firefox
options.rationale: A browser shows web pages.

options.text: A hypervisor, such as a VM host
options.rationale: A hypervisor runs virtual machines.

explanation: Configuration management tools such as Ansible, Puppet, Chef and Salt apply a described state again and again, with the same result.

stem: Which of these are configuration management tools? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Ansible
options.rationale: Ansible applies a described configuration to machines.

options.text: Samba
options.rationale: Samba shares files with Windows.

options.text: Puppet
options.rationale: Puppet manages configuration from a description of the wanted state.

options.text: Inkscape
options.rationale: Inkscape draws vector graphics.

options.text: Moodle
options.rationale: Moodle is a learning platform.

explanation: Ansible, Puppet, Chef and Salt are well-known configuration management tools.

stem: Why is it useful that a configuration management tool reads the wanted state from text files?

options.text: The files turn into graphical dialogs that an administrator clicks through on each machine.
options.rationale: The state is described in files, not dialogs.

options.text: The files replace the need for any servers, because they run the services themselves.
options.rationale: The tools configure servers; they don’t replace them.

options.text: The files can be kept in Git, reviewed and reused: infrastructure as code.
options.rationale: Text files are easy to version.

options.text: The files can only be read by the tool’s vendor, and not by the administrators.
options.rationale: They are normal text files.

explanation: Because the description is a text file, it can be tracked, reviewed and applied again and again.

stem: Ansible, Puppet, Chef and Salt are examples of what kind of software?

options.text: Package managers for Debian-based systems
options.rationale: Debian’s package tools are `dpkg` and `apt`.

options.text: Configuration management tools
options.rationale: They apply a described state to many machines.

options.text: Hypervisors for running virtual machines
options.rationale: Hypervisors run VMs, which isn’t what these tools do.

options.text: Text editors that run in the terminal
options.rationale: Terminal editors include vi and nano.

explanation: Configuration management tools describe the wanted state of machines in files and apply it.

stem: After Mira set up ten servers by hand, their settings differ slightly. How does configuration management help with this?

options.text: It sets all passwords to the same value on every server.
options.rationale: That would be a security problem, not configuration management.

options.text: A description applied again and again leaves every machine in the same state.
options.rationale: The same file gives the same result on every machine.

options.text: It replaces the kernel on every machine with a newer one.
options.rationale: It applies the described state, not a new kernel.

options.text: It turns every server into a virtual machine automatically.
options.rationale: It doesn’t change what kind of machine it is.

explanation: Hand-made setups drift apart; a description applied repeatedly keeps all machines in the same state.

stem: Which password is the best choice for a studio account?

options.text: A random passphrase of unrelated words, 16 characters or more, used for one account
options.rationale: Long, random and unique is stronger than short and clever.

options.text: Pixel2024!, which is easy to remember and has a symbol in it
options.rationale: It is short and predictable.

options.text: The studio’s name with the year after it, so that everyone on the team remembers it easily
options.rationale: It can be guessed from public facts.

options.text: The same strong password on all accounts, so that only one has to be remembered
options.rationale: Reuse means one leak exposes every account.

explanation: Length beats cleverness. A strong password is long, random or made of unrelated words, and unique.

stem: Why does the studio’s team use a password manager?

options.text: It lets them reuse one single password everywhere without any risk to their accounts.
options.rationale: Reuse is a problem it helps avoid.

options.text: It makes passwords unnecessary on all sites, because the vault logs in for them.
options.rationale: Passkeys do that; a manager stores passwords.

options.text: It sends passwords to colleagues by email so that the whole team shares one login.
options.rationale: Passwords should never be sent by email.

options.text: It keeps many unique passwords in an encrypted vault that one master password opens.
options.rationale: It can also create random passwords and fill them in.

explanation: A password manager is an encrypted store of passwords. Open source ones exist, such as KeePassXC and Bitwarden.

stem: Which two are factors for multi-factor authentication? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The user name
options.rationale: The user name identifies you; it is not a secret.

options.text: The name of the site
options.rationale: It is not a secret proof of identity.

options.text: A second password that is the same as the first
options.rationale: It is the same kind of factor: something you know.

options.text: A fingerprint
options.rationale: That is something you are.

options.text: An authenticator app code on a phone
options.rationale: That is something you have.

explanation: Factors are something you know, something you have and something you are. Two factors from different kinds are far safer than one.

stem: Which statement about passkeys is correct?

options.text: A passkey is a long random password that a password manager types in for you automatically.
options.rationale: A passkey isn’t a password.

options.text: A passkey is a code that is sent by text message.
options.rationale: That is an SMS code.

options.text: The website stores a public key; the private key stays on your device, unlocked by a PIN.
options.rationale: Passkeys resist phishing, since there is no password to type.

options.text: A passkey is a list of backup answers to security questions.
options.rationale: Passkeys are public-key credentials.

explanation: Passkeys use public-key cryptography, and can sync between devices or be tied to a hardware key.

stem: Ada receives an email that looks like it comes from the studio’s bank and links to a login page. What is the risk?

options.text: A virus on a USB stick infects the server through the mail program.
options.rationale: That is another threat.

options.text: The password expires after exactly one year because the email says so.
options.rationale: Expiry isn’t the risk.

options.text: The browser stops working until the email is deleted from the inbox.
options.rationale: The page being fake is the risk.

options.text: Phishing: typing her password on a fake site hands it to an attacker.
options.rationale: Passkeys and a password manager help against this, since they won’t fill in a fake site.

explanation: Typical password problems are weak or short passwords, reuse, writing them down, sharing them and phishing.

stem: Jonas wants to know whether the shop page he is about to pay on is encrypted in transit. What should he check?

options.text: The page loads quickly and looks the same as the shop’s paper catalogue.
options.rationale: Speed says nothing about encryption.

options.text: The address starts with `https://` and a lock symbol is shown.
options.rationale: HTTPS is HTTP wrapped in TLS, with a certificate.

options.text: The page has a lot of images and a famous brand’s logo at the top.
options.rationale: Images say nothing about security.

options.text: The address starts with `http://` and the shop’s name appears in it.
options.rationale: Plain HTTP isn’t encrypted.

explanation: HTTPS encrypts the traffic and the browser checks the server’s certificate.

stem: Mira’s laptop is lost on a train. Which measure protects the files on its disk?

options.text: A longer user name
options.rationale: A user name doesn’t protect files on a disk.

options.text: Using HTTPS for web pages
options.rationale: HTTPS protects data in transit, not on the disk.

options.text: Full-disk encryption with a strong passphrase
options.rationale: Encrypted data is useless without the key.

options.text: A bigger hard disk
options.rationale: Size has no security effect.

explanation: On Linux the usual tool is LUKS, set up with `cryptsetup`. The passphrase must be strong.

stem: Why is `ssh` preferred over the old `telnet` for logging in to a remote machine?

options.text: ssh encrypts the connection; telnet sends everything as plain text.
options.rationale: Anyone on the way could read telnet traffic.

options.text: ssh works without any network connection, directly through the keyboard.
options.rationale: Both need a network.

options.text: telnet is newer and uses a stronger password.
options.rationale: telnet is the old plaintext protocol.

options.text: ssh only works for the root user and never for ordinary accounts.
options.rationale: ssh works for ordinary users.

explanation: Encrypted network protocols such as HTTPS and ssh protect data in transit.

stem: Jonas finds a USB stick on the studio’s parking lot. What should he do?

options.text: Plug it into the build server to see what is on it.
options.rationale: That risks the most important machine.

options.text: Not plug it in; it might carry malware
options.rationale: Unknown sticks can be a trick.

options.text: Run the programs on it to find the owner.
options.rationale: Running unknown programs is dangerous.

options.text: Copy its files to the shared drive.
options.rationale: That spreads possible malware.

explanation: Don’t plug in found or unknown USB devices, scan files from sticks, encrypt private ones and eject them before pulling them out.

stem: Which two habits make USB sticks safer? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Run any program from a stick you were handed.
options.rationale: Unknown programs may be malware.

options.text: Turn on auto-running so that sticks start by themselves.
options.rationale: Auto-running should be turned off.

options.text: Encrypt sticks that carry private data.
options.rationale: A lost stick then doesn’t expose the data.

options.text: Keep the only copy of your files on the stick.
options.rationale: Sticks are easy to lose, so keep backups.

options.text: Eject (unmount) a stick before pulling it out.
options.rationale: That makes sure the data is fully written.

explanation: Encrypt, scan, eject and back up.

stem: Which tool is a privacy tool that hides your traffic from the local network and shows its own address to websites?

options.text: A VPN
options.rationale: A VPN moves your trust to the VPN company.

options.text: A cookie
options.rationale: Cookies are small files that sites store in your browser.

options.text: A password manager
options.rationale: A manager stores passwords.

options.text: A spreadsheet
options.rationale: A spreadsheet isn’t a privacy tool.

explanation: Privacy tools include a password manager, a browser with tracking protection, an encrypted messenger, GPG, disk encryption and a VPN.

stem: What is a cookie in a web browser?

options.text: A program in the browser that blocks advertising on websites.
options.rationale: That is a content blocker.

options.text: A bookmark of a favourite page that the browser keeps in a list on the toolbar.
options.rationale: Bookmarks are saved links.

options.text: A small file a site stores in your browser, used for logins and tracking
options.rationale: Cookies remember logins and can track you across sites.

options.text: An encrypted connection to a site, shown by a lock next to the address.
options.rationale: That is HTTPS.

explanation: You can block third-party cookies or delete cookies on exit.

stem: Jonas uses a private (incognito) window in his browser. What does it do?

options.text: It hides all his traffic from the internet provider and from his employer.
options.rationale: It does not hide traffic from the provider.

options.text: It makes the connection to every website encrypted with a stronger key.
options.rationale: Encryption depends on HTTPS.

options.text: It stops websites from seeing his address.
options.rationale: Sites still see his address.

options.text: It keeps no history or cookies on his computer, but doesn’t hide him from sites.
options.rationale: It stops the history from being kept locally.

explanation: Private mode only avoids local traces.

stem: Mira prepares a presentation for a school talk using only open source programs. Which program creates the slides?

options.text: Inkscape
options.rationale: Inkscape draws vector graphics.

options.text: LibreOffice Impress
options.rationale: Impress is the presentation program of LibreOffice.

options.text: Thunderbird
options.rationale: Thunderbird is an email client.

options.text: VLC
options.rationale: VLC plays media files.

explanation: Writer, Calc and Impress cover reports, spreadsheets and slides. A PDF can be saved for any computer.

stem: Ada opens a Linux desktop she has never used. Which part launches programs and which part manages files?

options.text: The terminal emulator is the only way to start any program on the desktop.
options.rationale: Desktops offer a launcher or menu.

options.text: The package manager shows folders as windows.
options.rationale: That is the job of a file manager.

options.text: The kernel draws the file manager’s icons.
options.rationale: Icons are drawn by the desktop.

options.text: A launcher or menu starts programs; the file manager handles files.
options.rationale: Most desktops have a launcher, a way to switch windows, a file manager and settings.

explanation: GNOME, KDE Plasma and Xfce look different but offer the same kinds of tools.

stem: Jonas wants to reach the shell on his Linux desktop. What can he open in a window?

options.text: A terminal emulator
options.rationale: A terminal emulator is a program that runs a shell in a window.

options.text: A file manager
options.rationale: A file manager shows files.

options.text: A web browser
options.rationale: A browser shows web pages.

options.text: A hypervisor
options.rationale: A hypervisor runs virtual machines.

explanation: Ctrl+Alt+T opens a terminal on many desktops.

stem: What is a virtual console?

options.text: A window on the desktop that runs a shell for you, which is a terminal emulator.
options.rationale: That is a terminal emulator.

options.text: A remote login over the network using `ssh` from another machine.
options.rationale: That is done with `ssh`.

options.text: A text-only screen from the kernel, reached with keys such as Ctrl+Alt+F2.
options.rationale: You can switch between virtual consoles.

options.text: A virtual machine that runs a shell.
options.rationale: It isn’t a machine.

explanation: The console was originally the physical keyboard and screen. A terminal is any text interface.

stem: Mira asks the guest for the device name of the terminal she is typing in. What does this command print?

options.text: /dev/pts/0
options.rationale: The terminal is a pseudo-terminal, so `tty` prints its device.

options.text: /dev/tty1
options.rationale: `/dev/tty1` is the first virtual console, not a pseudo-terminal.

options.text: /dev/sda
options.rationale: `/dev/sda` is a disk.

options.text: /dev/null
options.rationale: `/dev/null` discards data.

explanation: The terminal in this app is a pseudo-terminal, and `tty` prints its device name.

stem: What does this command print in the guest’s terminal?
explanation: `TERM` tells programs which kind of terminal the shell has; xterm.js reports `xterm-256color`.

stem: Which command prints the file name of the terminal connected to your shell? Type the command.
explanation: `tty` prints the device name of the terminal, for example `/dev/pts/0`.

stem: Which statement about the words terminal and console is correct?

options.text: A terminal is always a physical device with a screen, and a console is only software.
options.rationale: It is the other way round.

options.text: The console was the machine’s own keyboard and screen; a terminal is any text interface.
options.rationale: A terminal emulator pretends to be one inside a window.

options.text: They are the same as a desktop environment.
options.rationale: A desktop is graphical.

options.text: A console is a remote machine in the cloud.
options.rationale: It isn’t.

explanation: The terms overlap, and in practice people use both for the text interface.
